facts.claim: "Shake! Shake! Shake!" is credited to The Deadbeat Cousins & Liam St. John and was released as a single on 2022-11-11, with a running time of 3:08.
Deezer lists the writers and composers as Jaren Glade Soelberg, Jess Alan Soelberg, Matthew Parry Shaker, Jason James Roedl and Shannon Liam St. John.
Liam St. John is a Los Angeles-based blues and blues rock musician. Viberate lists this song as one of his collaborations with The Deadbeat Cousins.
Viberate describes the track as combining St. John's soulful vocals with the band's blues rock sound, a hard-rocking rhythm section and guitar riffs.

The Deadbeat Cousins formed in Phoenix, Arizona in 2017. The core members are Matt Shaker (vocals, guitar), Jaren Soelberg (guitar), Jess Soelberg (bass) and Jason Roedl (drums). Jess Soelberg is related to Jaren.
Shaker and Soelberg have been friends since seventh grade, but they had not collaborated on music until they started the Cousins.
The band chose its name in a brainstorming session, settling on Deadbeat Cousins over Coyote Cousins.
The band's debut album Get By came out in 2019. Old Habits followed on September 23, 2022, about seven weeks before this single. Both were released on the band's own label, The Deadbeat Cousins.
The band's Bandsintown bio says they play blues rock "because we like it when the rooms shake a bit". It also says bassist Jess moved to Nashville, leaving a four-piece.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Arizona (Phoenix/Mesa) blues-rock scene, in a style sources describe as drawing on classic blues and rock traditions with modern alternative and indie rock touches.

draft:
A chorus built on three verbs, shake, pay, take, keeps a ledger for a life going under. **Shake! Shake! Shake!** opens that ledger with a child's piggy bank, the narrator dropping in a penny, and then admits where the real money went: "My last dime I wasted on an alibi." It's a small, sharp confession. Not spent on a drink or a debt, but on a story to cover something. The guilt is already in the purchase.

What makes the song sting is that the narrator can't decide whose fault this is. The verses point outward. Someone left without a word, someone plotted the downfall and spun the web the narrator walked straight into. Then the chorus turns the finger around: "Now I'm payin' for all my mistakes," and the bill comes due "One drink at a time." That last phrase bends the recovery-room mantra about taking things one day at a time into a slow, deliberate slide. Blame and self-blame sit next to each other and never settle, which is how it actually feels to be left and to know you helped it happen.

The fourth verse makes that tension plainer. The narrator talks about being bleached and purified, then lists gasoline and lines in the same breath, and ends by saying they're fixing to stay high. Cleanness is the wish, and the wish loses. By the bridge there's nothing left to argue over. "What's yours, it isn't mine" reads like a settlement signed out of exhaustion, the dotted line in the previous line making it sound almost legal. Then the chorus returns, and the song closes by repeating its drink-at-a-time line until it sounds like a habit rather than a hook.

The band plays all of this steady and unhurried. Strummed acoustic guitar sits under a clean electric line that picks out single notes. A walking bass and a snare-heavy rock beat give it a driving pulse with a slight swing. The room is dry and close, the sound polished without being slick. Liam St. John sings it alone, with no harmonies, clear and conversational, as if laying out the accounts to someone across a table.

The Deadbeat Cousins came together in Phoenix in 2017, built around Matt Shaker and Jaren Soelberg, friends since seventh grade, and they've said they play blues rock because they like it when the rooms shake a bit. Their debut album was called Get By, and the first verse here admits they're still trying to. The credits list all five writers, St. John among them, and the song arrived seven weeks after their second record, Old Habits.

It sticks because it lets you be angry at someone and ashamed of yourself in the same chorus, and it never makes you choose.
